rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation is in `inclusive_scan_kernel` at line 30. However, `parallel_scan_cuda` (the only entry point) ONLY launches `row_scan_kernel`: `row_scan_kernel<float><<<outer_elements, threads, shared_mem_size>>>(x_ptr, out_ptr, outer_elements, n);`. The `inclusive_scan_kernel` is defined but NEVER INVOKED anywhere in the code. The mutation is in dead code.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutant survives because the mutation exists in a kernel function (`inclusive_scan_kernel`) that is never called. The `parallel_scan_cuda` function, which is the only entry point from Python, exclusively launches `row_scan_kernel` for computation. The `inclusive_scan_kernel` appears to be leftover/template code that was defined but not integrated into the actual execution path. Since the mutated line is inside an unused function, no input values of any shape or magnitude can ever trigger the mutated code path. This makes the mutant semantically equivalent to the original under all possible inputs.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable - the mutation is in dead code (an unused kernel function). No value-level test can kill this mutant because `inclusive_scan_kernel` is never executed. Only a code change that actually calls `inclusive_scan_kernel` would expose the mutation, which violates the fixed-shape contract.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should include static dead-code analysis to detect mutations in unreachable code paths before expensive runtime testing. In this case, a simple call-graph analysis would reveal that `inclusive_scan_kernel` has no callers, allowing immediate classification as an equivalent mutant without any runtime tests.
